lessons: The app did not start its own Dev engine (launchd needs LWCR update with ad-hoc signing); first launch fell on a stale error screen.
Quit stops Silo-owned local computers but never computers on other devices.
launchd refuses ad-hoc-signed Dev engine builds ('needs LWCR update'), so live checks start silod directly.
SSH starts the bridge through a ~/.local/bin link where macOS finds no bundle; the process must re-exec from its real path.
The runtime socket path must stay under 104 bytes, which caps the HOME length at 28 bytes.
Linux computers are detached runtime processes, so an engine exit need not kill them; systemd KillMode=process is required to keep that true.
A session end that leaves a computer running must exit non-zero so the supervisor records it.
Ctrl-C in a terminal reached msb children too; start them in their own process group.
190 calls in 37 groups grew partly because app screens got their own calls (display.viewer.*, exports.dismiss); a rewrite should keep calls per user action.
Events are not yet cut per computer, so a computer's agent cannot subscribe and has to poll.
Each MicroSandbox upgrade found regressions (missing runtime_instance_id, restore with spare CPU or memory, relay disconnect during a bulk write); keep upgrade checks.
msb needs the library-validation exception to load libkrunfw without an Apple Team ID.
A nested source checkout needs its own Git repository, or patches silently skip paths.
Upstream restore always starts the guest and create always boots; stopped create and fork needed patches.
Snapshot capture folders were never deleted upstream, so deleting snapshots freed no disk.
Compaction upstream kept the old layers, using more disk instead of less.
Upstream 0.7.14 made blocked connections complete with a 403; Silo refuses them so nothing is ever sent to an unlisted address.
The VM is the wall, not the guest account: the silo working account has passwordless sudo.
Bundling the image made installers about 440 MiB instead of 35 MiB; download on first use.
The runtime's image load does not accept an outer gzip stream.
Publish the guest image release before the app release that pins it, since the app downloads it directly.
The image import lock is in-process only; a cross-process lock is missing.
Build tools had to stream archives instead of loading them into memory.
A computer cannot stop or delete itself; an agent may only stop or delete computers it made.
A running fork must be stopped before it can be dropped (M E3), which agents trip over.
A computer cannot stop or delete itself; an agent works only on computers it made.
M: a macOS computer made with `silo create --macos` never appeared in the app's list.
A running fork must be stopped before it can be dropped (journey 2 gap).
On macOS the account group is staff, which every account shares; tokens must be 0600 owner-only there.
A one-shot exec is capped at 180 s by the engine; long work needs the streaming form.
A process still running when the engine died is not tracked after restart; its job reads back as lost.
Commands travel as argv, never shell source, except one carefully quoted line over SSH for macOS.
Keep one operations layer that both the CLI and MCP call, returning the same JSON, so the two never drift.
Exit codes are a contract agents script against; changing one breaks callers silently.
Never touch the production link from a Dev build; names come from one channel module.
The editor/terminal command is built by the engine from a fixed agent list; nothing else can be named.
Showing the SSH name adds an Include line to ~/.ssh/config as a side effect (V G3c).
Write only an included file, never the user's ~/.ssh/config body.
Key aliases by computer id, never by name.
Unsupported terminals must fail clearly instead of opening a local shell that looks like success.
Ghostty needs Automation permission and the Apple Events entitlement.
A failed start leaves the computer Stopped; keep the result of the request separate from the computer's state, keyed by computer id.
Names and disk sizes are fixed after creation; only CPU and memory can change.
Operations and events cover every computer and are not cut per caller, so agents cannot use them.
Losing the client connection while waiting must never turn into a failed job.
The UI decides from the operation kind the engine reports, never from label text.
The gate does not nest, so long operations (rebuild, promote) must hold it once and call un-gated helpers.
It does not replace the OS file lock between runtime processes.
A saved configuration journal must block snapshots only while an attempt is live, or one failed attempt freezes the computer list until relaunch.
Detached runtime children own MicroSandbox's lifecycle guards, not Silo's command lock.
The lock descriptor was inherited by every process it started, including the VM, so it outlived the engine.
Test parsers against real launchctl output, not the format a bug report described.
Holding a global mutex across remote calls deadlocked the app.
DNS queries are an unfiltered outbound channel; rebind protection does not stop connecting by IP.
QUIC (UDP 443) is dropped so all HTTPS goes through the proxy.
A LAN host with a public or global IPv6 address counts as public.
DNS rebinding to private addresses is blocked, but DNS itself remains an outbound channel.
Only the exact production identifier selects production, so a stray build can never touch production data.
Keychain is absent under another HOME, so checks needing saved sign-ins cannot use their own instance.
Only the real engine on the KVM runner showed several container bugs; keep a real-VM job in CI.
An interrupted checkpoint could block the next start until its dependencies were released (R10).
A computer's agent checkpointing itself always makes a manual checkpoint so retention never removes the owner's automatic and step checkpoints.
Restore first saves a recovery checkpoint and leaves the computer stopped.
Forking an earlier checkpoint of itself asks the owner: it can hold access since taken away.
Snapshot data and its graph belong to MicroSandbox; Silo keeps only names, intent and references, and removes without --force so upstream guards still apply.
A snapshot something still needs (a fork not started yet, an import, a restore's recovery point) must be pinned by Silo records.
A fork must drop the source's Silo-tools token and get its own endpoint, or it answers as its parent (T5b S3).
A fork may get only what the caller already has; forking an earlier checkpoint of itself asks, since it can hold what the owner since took away.
A fork always cold-boots the disks, never memory, so nothing of the source keeps running.
The engine does not copy published ports; the CLI republishes them, each on its own device port.
Early plan said forks stay stopped until an explicit Start; the CLI later starts them by default.
Upstream restore always starts the guest, so a stopped fork is a Silo record pointing at an immutable snapshot until Start.
The pending restore is consumed only after a durable successful start; a failed first start must not cold-boot or double-start.
Other tools have placeholder secrets, allowlists and microVMs; only the whole-machine loop is distinctive, so it is what comes first.
MicroSandbox has no hook to edit a snapshot's disk before boot, so the quiet script runs from Silo's boot hook first and the engine confirms its marker after start.
Match process names by exact base name, never by pattern.
Login-time programs and file-stored secrets are not covered; scrub is the answer for files.
A memory snapshot copies logins that a token proxy cannot remove, so forks are disk only.
A fork is stopped and never runs briefly as a side effect.
About 9.8 s and 0.5 GiB per Linux fork, 59 s per macOS fork, measured on one M4 Max.
MicroSandbox has no hook to edit a snapshot before boot; quieting runs from a boot hook carried in the runtime patch.
Shell profiles and login-started programs are not covered.
Lineage must be read through the replace-main journal, or forks of the old main point at the wrong computer.
Being forked from a computer does not make it that computer's agent's: only computers it made are in its tree.
Silo's own files (endpoint.json, pulse files) must be ignored or every fork conflicts on them (M C2).
Silo's own per-computer files (/etc/silo, receipts, machine ids) must be on the ignore list or every fork shows them as changes.
Item ids are built only from what names the item, so the same id works in diff, conflict and choice.
Idle macOS forks rewrite many preference and database files; they need a built-in ignore list.
Databases are shown but not driven live.
guest.exec is capped at 768 KiB and 180 s, so the collector runs detached in the guest and is read back in chunks.
A known record with too few fields is an error, because a truncated stream would otherwise read as deleted files.
The fork-time base is captured at the fork's first start, after the quiet step and before it reports ready.
A database is never combined; only one side is taken.
Keeping a fork without asking when its tests pass was dropped: the tests run in the fork, so the fork can fake them.
An agent merging into its own computer asks the owner and must carry the digest of a diff it ran.
A Linux merge reads and writes as root; run repo commands as the folder's owner.
Hash both computers live at merge time; a file the collector could not hash is never taken as unchanged.
A journal synced before main changes lets the next merge, undo or engine start restore an interrupted merge.
Databases are never combined: a database change needs the recipe's migrate step or an explicit data-ok.
A request whose fork changed after it was made must be refused; the agent asks again.
Undo restores everything since the merge, including unrelated work like agents installed afterwards (V I3b).
Undo of a replace only reverts the latest one involving either computer.
A before-merge checkpoint becomes undoable only after its merge succeeded, and is consumed once restored.
A .env file that Git ignores is carried without a credential check; the wall covers Git history only.
An install on an allowlist network fails; the error must say the network blocks it (V G1b).
Install folders must be readable by the working account (Codex /opt/silo/codex was 0700).
An allowlist network blocks agent install; say which hosts are needed.
Never report missing for a computer Silo could not ask; that is unknown.
On macOS, copy the staged file into a root-only folder before checking its hash, so the account cannot swap it.
One loopback port per computer plus a token only that computer holds; the network allows exactly that port.
The engine puts the shipped program back at each start if an agent replaces or deletes it.
The peer address is always 127.0.0.1, so only the token tells computers apart; never send the token itself, prove it per nonce and port.
Any program on the device can connect to the loopback port; on a shared Linux host this is weaker than single-user.
The earlier /.msb request-file bridge needed holds and cache dropping around checkpoints and did not exist for macOS; it was removed.
A loopback TCP port has no owner: any account can connect or take it while the engine is down, so the token is the identity.
Keep a port that is no longer a computer's bound with an accept-and-close listener until the computer restarts without it.
Device-only tools (up, ssh_name, request_open) are hidden inside a computer; secrets and export/import are never MCP tools.
A new method must not compile until it is classified for the computer caller.
Lists that cover every computer (operations, events, notifications) were refused to agents because they were not cut per caller yet.
'Made by', not lineage, decides reach: a fork the owner made by hand may hold more than its parent.
After replace main the made-by records must move, or the old main keeps control of the new one.
A computer with no saved network policy must be judged closed, not open (imports).
Any same-user process on the device is the owner today; programs on the device have no identity yet.
A fork you made by hand from main may hold more than main, so lineage is not authority.
What a computer may touch is decided by a recorded created_by, not by lineage: a fork you made by hand may hold more access than its parent.
The summary must come from the call's parameters, never from the agent's text.
Approvals are answered on the device whose computer asked.
Write the summary from the call's parameters, never the agent's words, and strip control characters and direction overrides from anything the agent chose.
An allowed call is checked again as if just made, then run from the stored copy.
Limits: 30 an hour, 20 waiting, seven-day expiry; a secret value is removed from the file when the approval ends.
Summaries are written by the engine from parameters, never from the agent's words; agent text is stripped of control and direction characters.
An allow is recorded first and never re-run on its own after a crash.
Deny on a merge approval must close the review request too, or it comes back as its own row.
Visible delivery in Notification Center was never verified; policy and authorization were tested natively.
The Tauri notification plugin has no desktop click callback or replace-by-id, so UNUserNotificationCenter is used directly.
The panel window and its page must both be transparent or a second rectangular outline shows.
Native corner and tray clicks were never driven by automation.
Asking for approval on size was dropped: the agent sizes from what resources shows and the floor refuses.
The owner asked for no hard caps on computers; only a floor that prevents freezing the device.
Admitted starts should reserve memory so a burst cannot pass the floor together (owed).
The check and the hold must be under one lock, or concurrent approved starts slip past the floor.
A burst of starts could each pass the floor before any computer took memory, so jobs reserve memory until the computer runs or 2 hours pass.
Restart, undo and restore of a running computer keep its memory set aside, so they need no free memory.
Open: whether the app shows a resource pane.
A Dev app can open on 'Silo could not load' after an older engine left its record (journey 1).
The dependency check screen was driven in a signed bundle on 2026-09-08; the full first run in today's app is not driven.
Setup must wait for real computer and GitHub acknowledgements; an earlier prototype faked progress with fixtures.
A removed runtime file was reported by exact name and Continue stayed disabled; keep that failure path tested.
All-repositories mode with an empty installation catalog gave zero credentials and silent 401s (044 investigation).
A fork gets only a read-only copy of GitHub access the caller's own access covers.
A scoped token cannot mint another scoped token; all minting happens from the host's user token.
'All repositories' with an empty catalog produced zero grants yet said verified; success must mean an authenticated request worked.
Never replay an ambiguous code exchange, refresh or mint; GitHub refresh tokens rotate and a consumed one is gone.
A hosted server was thought necessary; GitHub's PKCE with a public client secret made a server-free flow possible.
The shipped client secret is public by design; PKCE binds the code, so it is never proof of an authentic install.
'Verified' meant only that reconciliation finished; zero grants still showed success.
TLS must be intercepted only for hosts a secret is allowed for, or agents' own provider calls fail certificate checks (ZCODE-TLS).
An unmatched placeholder must pass through unchanged: blocking it stalled agents that echoed it into model requests (AGENT-PLACEHOLDER-STALL).
Values go to the runtime on stdin, never in arguments, config files or the environment.
Intercept TLS only for hosts a secret is allowed for; intercepting everything broke agents that drop inherited CA settings (ZCode).
An allowed host that echoes headers reveals the value; restrict hosts to services you trust.
Values reach the runtime on stdin, never in arguments, config or environment; secret names that would override proxy or loader variables are refused.
An unchanged placeholder an agent echoes in a request must pass through, or the TLS connection closes and every retry stalls.
Dev rebuilds lose Keychain access, which blocked every live secret check.
Silo cannot narrow a personal token, so a fork can never inherit one.
Updating policy after the guest resumes is too late; it must be applied before activation.
Folder names must be percent-encoded per segment, and names with control characters refused.
SSH and SFTP first ran in / instead of the home folder and SFTP returned failure after a good transfer; both fixed in the runtime patch.
When Silo cannot edit the user's SSH config it shows the exact Include line to add.
Offer only apps the handoff accepts (Xcode was the default editor on many Macs).
The URL crate silently drops tabs and newlines, changing the folder identity.
macOS agents open with ssh -F and a per-computer config so ~/.ssh/config stays untouched.
URL parsers drop tabs and newlines instead of encoding them, so refuse control characters in folder names or the editor opens another path.
OpenSSH refuses a private key with any group or other bits; repair modes to 0600.
Owner decided 2026-11-16 that T3 Code runs on the Mac and connects in; it does not run inside the computer.
The macOS template still contains Claude Code because changing it rebuilds every user's template.
A computer reads only the recipe it was built from (V I2b).
Any computer may fork the hidden silo-build- computer of a recipe, and gets nothing beyond what the caller has.
Package names and service commands reach build scripts only as environment variables, never as shell text.
A computer never sees a recipe's command lines, because the owner may have pasted a token there.
A rebuild keeps the old cache until the new build succeeds.
A macOS build needs one of the two macOS VM slots.
Package names are passed as arguments, never shell text; setup lines are shell text.
Tokens never go in setup or test lines: every computer built from it can read them.
Owner decided 2026-11-16 that a recipe sets up a whole working computer and that making one must be convenient.
The default Linux recipe has no Node, so most agent tooling needs setup before it runs.
Changing a published-site origin discards browser state, so the name-hash.localhost origins must not change.
A fork inherits its source's published port and asks to publish it again (V I3a).
`silo ports` inside a computer read network.state, which a computer may not call.
The upstream publisher did not forward guest EOF, so HTTP/1.0 responses hung; the patch forwards half-closes both ways.
Listening alone never marks a service reachable; a failed inspection is an error, never an empty list.
Never bind guest port numbers on the host: a user's own later server on :3000 would fail.
Safari resolves *.localhost only from macOS 26.
Origins are stored in browsers: changing the naming scheme discards their state.
A running computer keeps its previous rules until it restarts; the state says so.
A preset that grew in a newer Silo counts as wider and asks again.
Name lookups are blocked in closed mode too.
An allowlist does not stop sending data to a listed host, and DNS can still carry data out.
Presets can widen in a Silo update, so setting a grown preset asks again.
Save a narrowing only if the policy is still the one it was judged against.
A missing policy entry for a computer marked as having had one is damage, not an empty store; keep the mark outside the policy file.
Warn on *. patterns over names anyone can publish under (*.github.io); refuse them over registry suffixes (*.co.uk).
The stock exec command starts stopped computers; a --no-start patch was needed so browsing never boots one.
A hint is never authoritative: clients re-read.
Remote names reach sftp only through commands that do not expand wildcards; local sources are staged behind a fixed symlink name.
msb copy starts stopped computers and writes root-owned files, so system sftp was chosen.
Never verified against a real guest or a remote computer.
Never concatenate the diagnostic into the summary.
A leftover record from an older engine blocks a rebuilt Dev app at startup.
Silo never force-resets a repository; a repo conflict can only go to a branch or stay as main.
Silo never force-resets a repository: a conflicting one can only go to a branch or stay as main.
Fast-forward must not swap computers, because the agent lives in main.
Silo's own per-computer files and per-login files conflicted on every merge until left out.
Undo was flaky on Postgres sequences in v1.
Wire names keep 'keep' and 'fold' spellings while people read 'merge'; a rewrite should pick one word end to end.
A merge approval and its review request are linked; denying one must close the other.
Once linked to an approval only the engine writes the request's text.
The fork must be as it was when the agent asked; a moved change generation refuses and asks again.
From inside a computer it always asks, since it restarts the agent's own computer.
Tell sandboxes apart by the identity they carry (silo.machine-id), never by name, because a crash can leave names half moved.
Every step must be idempotent with a revert, so engine start can roll forward or back.
Lineage after a replace is read from the journal, not rewritten into the stores.
An agent's merge must never add packages that the owner's next rebuild installs on every computer from that recipe.
An agent's merge must change only that computer's record, never the owner's saved recipe.
A merge an agent ran changes the saved recipe only with the owner's approval, so recipes can fall behind.
Command lines are stored as typed, so secrets in arguments end up in the step list.
A step is a command run through Silo; edits over plain SSH are not seen.
macOS allows only two macOS VMs running at once; check slots before making forks.
MicroSandbox never deletes restored memory files under cache/memory/snapshots; Silo must remove files no checkpoint names.
A resource edit that invalidates saved memory needs an explicit disk-only decision; never drop memory silently.
Container computers have no memory in their checkpoints.
Each MicroSandbox snapshot holds its whole layer closure, so deleting old snapshots frees nothing until the disk's layers are compacted (msb modify --compact).
Export a capture without --with-parents: it writes a layer twice and snapshot load refuses it.
The merge of layers and the removal are one unit: a failed merge removes nothing.
Deleting snapshots frees nothing until layers are merged; never remove the newest, manual or depended-on ones.
A fresh snapshot group per export plus import created duplicate parents and broke later exports.
Cap the event file and keep a never-rotated counter summary, so a busy computer cannot grow it without bound.
Hooks a caller sends are ignored for a computer built from a recipe.
The push destination never comes from the fork; a fork's own origin naming another repo is refused.
Never measure a baseline on the used fork: its capture holds the task's own changes.
A recipe and a command cannot go in one call, and the computer stays running afterwards (journey 3 gap).
The pieces exist (fork with a command, merge --pr, review requests, the runner); what is missing is the layer that joins them into one unattended task.
The CI runner was set aside on 2026-11-10 because its general form (something outside starts a task in a fresh fork and gets the result) comes first.
Updating main after a pull request merges is an ordinary git pull, not a Silo feature (owner, 2026-11-16).
Keeping a fork without asking when its tests passed was removed: the tests ran inside the fork, which the agent controls as root, so it could fake them.
Anything an agent with root inside a computer reports about that computer (tests passed, tools OK) is its own claim and cannot gate a widening action.
The third journey starts from a recipe or a checkpoint so a task has no setup to wait for (owner, 2026-11-16).
GitHub sends no branch or SHA before giving a job, so one label must mean one recipe.
GitHub's own secrets and GITHUB_TOKEN go straight into the computer; Silo's placeholders do not protect them, so allow private repositories only.
Count capacity from a fresh list plus what is still forking; on a Mac every macOS VM counts toward Apple's two.
Runners are refused for public repositories: anyone's pull request could run a workflow on your Mac.
GitHub delivers its own secrets and GITHUB_TOKEN straight into the job, so Silo's placeholders do not protect them.
Lifecycle bugs (delete by name, retention before deregister) ended only with one owner of all state and a ledger by id, never by name.
An unsigned Linux engine directory must be owned and writable only by its account or root, all the way up from /, or anyone can swap the binaries.
Use KillMode=process: VM processes are detached on purpose so an update keeps them running.
Refuse to run as root or nobody; use a dedicated account in the kvm group.
sshd StrictModes ignores authorized_keys when home or ~/.ssh is group-writable; report the exact chmod.
Never run anything as root or turn lingering on; print the advice instead.
Existing .ssh modes survive key install unless repaired (review GB-01).
A default ACL made ssh-keygen write a world-readable key on the runner, so the engine sets 0600 itself.
Linux app builds and packages were discontinued; only the engine runs on Linux hosts.
Both devices must run the same remote protocol version; an updated one refuses the older and names it.
A computer's agent is refused any call that names another device.
Every Connections call silently failed for a long time because the forced command's flag had no caller after the engine moved; keep a live end-to-end check.
macOS refuses a socket timeout once the peer closed, about 1 call in 6, while the reply is still buffered: ignore it and read.
Both devices must run the same bridge protocol version; name which device to update.
A changed host key is never trusted from here; a typed fingerprint is the trust root.
Both devices must run the same protocol version; the newer one names the device to update.
`restrict` in authorized_keys disables TCP and socket forwarding together, so guest streams travel over the bridge, not SSH forwarding.
Prefer a --device flag over name@device so computer names stay plain.
Ports are published by the device a computer runs on; URLs differ per side.
A device never forwards a request on; each handler refuses a request that still names another device.
A retried change must attach to the original operation id, and a change not started before its deadline or after its controller left must never start.
An unrelated process can take a reserved port during SSH authentication; trust only `ssh -O check` on a private control socket before exposing the endpoint.
Turning access off is free for an agent; turning it on asks and states the address and key fingerprints.
Enabled does not mean listening: connections never start a stopped computer.
Measured fork costs (about 8 s, 0.2 to 0.5 GiB) come from one M4 Max with 64 GiB; capacity on other machines is unmeasured.
Keep passwords out of command arguments: a failed subprocess prints its arguments.
Stay below 1.0.0 until the owner decides; scripts refuse a stable version without a flag.
Apple's library constraints already work with ad-hoc signing: a hardened msb loads only the exact bundled libkrunfw.
The silo-ui build script printed the private GitHub build configuration into agent logs twice; a release script must never print configuration.
Never publish on an incomplete signature matrix or overwrite version assets; a dry run must not create a tag.
An embedded engine checks its signer requirement at run time, written into Info.plist before signing.
Release archives must contain only the Silo.app root; BSD tar's AppleDouble entries broke the first archive.
Losing the updater private key strands every installed app.
Hold the installer lock until the new package is in place; the engine's watchdog aborts the update if the app dies.
A rebuild in progress makes Quit and updates wait.
The runtime's discard-by-truncate optimisation shrank disks; a vendored fix keeps disk length while punching holes.
msb-imago truncated a disk when discard reached its end, shrinking it until mount failed with EINVAL; discard must punch holes and keep length.
Report reclaimed bytes from host allocation, not what fstrim prints.
A runtime tail-discard bug shrank disks on reopen; the fix is in Silo's patch.
A kill during create or rebuild left saved configuration and runtime state disagreeing; recovery must be designed in, not patched (R10).
Quit must not wait for a whole rebuild (T15).
Owned disk size must match exactly at start; layered disks need the whole owned-volumes folder moved.
Copy the home by tar inside the guest and msb cp, not exec output (10 MB/s).
Homes over about 45 % of the root disk are refused, because the home travels as a tar file.
The old computer never runs again after the workspace disk is cloned, so nothing it does can be missed.
A rebuild is refused when the home is over 45 % of the root disk, because the home is packed inside the computer before it moves.
Writes to the home in the seconds between packing and stopping are only in <name>-undo.
Follow must continue the previous snapshot, not start a new search every 3 seconds.
One malformed or 1 MiB record used to break every query for a computer.
Admission guards are bound to the thread that took them, so one dedicated thread must own the whole update transaction.
An old engine relaunched by the service manager during an install must not resume computers behind the installer.
Write the resume intent (resumeArmed) before exit, because a restore with --cow-mem resumes the guest by itself.
Update installation must change the app only, never computer disks; record the running set durably before stopping anything.
The login switch shows what macOS reports, never the saved flag; Requires approval stays off with an Open System Settings action.
Start at launch once started nothing because the saved switch had no computer list; the default must be resolved at startup.
Quit must ask the window to flush queued edits before exiting, or the last edit is lost.
A corrupt or future-version settings file is protected from all writes for the session instead of being overwritten.
Show plain actions, not method names (M finding 2).
Per-computer row caps keep one computer from pushing out other rows.
Refused handshakes are rate-limited to one row a second so a hostile program cannot flood the log.
A computer cannot push out other callers' rows.
Identical repeated rows collapse into one with a count, so a refusal loop cannot fill the log.
Each computer has its own row share (20,000) apart from owner and device rows, so a busy computer cannot push them out.
Activity first showed internal method names; plain words and hidden bookkeeping calls came after the live run.
Every blocked attempt is paired with one that must succeed, or the verdict is inconclusive, never pass.
The canary and secret are sent hex-encoded so the scanner cannot find its own arguments.
Only two runs exist (2026-11-03, Dev 0.11.1, Linux guests); macOS computers and the allowlist were never evaluated.
GitHub's hosted macOS runners are VMs that cannot start nested VMs, so they cannot run a Silo computer.
The guest serves the viewer's JavaScript, so only Silo's own UI may start a clipboard or file transfer.
Output is capped (64 KiB errors, 960 KiB runs) and never written to the device's disk.
Registering a Rust command does not grant it; each window's capability file must list it.
Restoring a checkpoint replaces the disk, not what the agent already sent.
One maintainer, so fixes can take longer than the acknowledgement.
The channel token is valid only on its own computer's port, so a copy of it in a fork or an export proves nothing.
A restore resets the runtime's network rules unless they are all passed again, so restore and fork rebuild them from the stored policy.
The old /.msb file-polling bridge was replaced; the share still has no security review.
The guest can change files the host later reads there (checkpoint state, heartbeat); Silo parses nothing from it but the share has had no security review.
A fork keeps its parent's login because the same agent already controls both.
It needs signed releases, which wait; computers do not need it because their identity is their channel.
Same-user malware stays a non-goal: identity makes actions attributable, it does not make that case safe.
The runtime runs as the user's own process without the App Sandbox, so a VM escape gives the user's account.
The rules that were in .silo/silo.yaml became policy set in the app because the agent could edit a file in its own repository.
In allowlist mode, DNS to another resolver is answered by Silo's own resolver; DNS-over-TLS to another resolver is refused because the gateway cannot complete TLS as that resolver.
Every boundary has been checked only by its author and by AI reviewers.
Docs that no longer describe the code are deleted, not archived (owner, 2026-11-15).
A computer with its desktop off held its operation lane for 5 minutes after start waiting for a session, making its first fork take 288 s.
Selkies 2.0.0 lets one page hold the display; a second page kills the first with a final close.
A Linux recipe with desktop: false cannot have services, because services start with the desktop session.
desktop.action also installs Node and Claude Code (SetupAgentTools), which belongs with agents install.
WKWebView's user agent lacks the Safari token, so KasmVNC read the clipboard on every click and macOS showed a Paste prompt.
The viewer moved from KasmVNC to Selkies 2.0.0; its settings come from localStorage, not URL parameters.
